list.listitem: The diagnosis of atopic dermatitis (AD) is primarily based on history and clinical presentation of disease; there is no definitive diagnostic test. C
Findings that best rule in diagnosis are onset before age 2, visible flexural eczema, and history of itchy, dry skin. C
Asthma, food, and environmental allergies are commonly associated with AD. B
Emollients are recommended for chronic maintenance therapy and should be continued during flares in all patients with AD. A

Use topical corticosteroids (TCS) as first-line treatment during acute flares in children and adults. Moderate - to high-potency TCS are more effective than low-potency TCS for moderate to severe AD. A

Another first-line option for treating flares and for maintenance, especially for sensitive skin (eg, face, anogenital, and intertriginous areas), is topical tacrolimus 0.1% ointment. It is as effective as moderate- to high-potency TCS, and is superior to pimecrolimus and low-potency TCS. A

Topical Janus-associated kinase (JAK) inhibitors, A topical phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) inhibitors, B and topical aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) agonists B are second-line options for moderately severe AD but may be cost-prohibitive.

background.definition: Atopic dermatitis (AD) or eczema is a chronic inflammatory pruritic skin disease affecting children and adults.

list.listitem: Incidence rates increased worldwide beginning in the 1960s and vary considerably within countries and geographical areas.
AD affects 10% to 20% of children and 1% to 3% of adults.
Sleep loss is common for patients and their parents, with an average sleep loss of 2 hours per night.
Other significant social/behavioral problems include irritability, daytime tiredness, fearfulness, mood changes, dependence, and missed school/work days.
AD is associated with a small but significant increase in depressive symptoms and suicidal thoughts.
It is also associated with an increased risk of acute otitis media, pharyngitis, urinary tract infections, anxiety and depression.
AD is characterized by a defect in the skin barrier system along with an increase in inflammatory cytokines and IgE levels.
Family and sibling studies have demonstrated a genetic predisposition to AD.
Food and airborne allergens may play a pathogenic role.

AD is the result of multiple factors including genetic predisposition, defect in the skin barrier system, abnormal response to normal skin flora, and dysregulation of both innate and adaptive immunity.
Loss of function of the filaggrin gene, a key component in the epidermal barrier, predisposes to AD.
There is a strong genetic predisposition to asthma, AD, and GERD.
Staphylococcus aureus colonizes the skin of 95% of AD patients (<5% in controls), with increased concentration in areas affected by AD.
Maternal antigen avoidance (eg, cow's milk, eggs) during pregnancy or lactation does not appear to decrease the incidence of AD in infants. B

Exclusive breastfeeding of any duration does not decrease the incidence of AD in children beyond 2 years of life. A systematic review of 6 cohort studies suggests that exclusive breastfeeding in the first 3 to 4 months of life may decrease the incidence of AD in children up to 2 years. B
Delaying introduction of solid foods until after 6 months of age does not reduce the risk of AD in children. B
Early complementary feeding of infants age 12 to 16 weeks with peanut, cow's milk, wheat, and egg does not appear to prevent AD at 12 months. B
Probiotic or synbiotic (probiotic with added prebiotic) have uncertain benefits in preventing the development of atopy by two years of age and during childhood up to 10 years of age. B
Hydrolyzed infant formula or soy formula does not appear to prevent AD compared with standard infant formula or breast milk. B

Supplementing formula-fed infants with prebiotics (mixture of immunoactive oligosaccharides) appears better than standard infant formula at preventing AD at 1 year (5.7% vs 9.7%, P <.01, NNT = 25). However, breastfeeding appears comparable to prebiotics supplementation for preventing AD. B
Polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation during pregnancy, lactation or infancy to prevent AD is supported by limited evidence, hence it should not be given routinely. B
Daily use of emollients during infancy does not prevent AD in healthy or high-risk infants and may increase risk of skin infections. B
Exposure to pets, dogs in particular, may reduce the risk of developing AD. B
Findings that best rule in AD, when present, are onset before age 2, visible flexural eczema, and history of itchy, dry skin. C

Both major diagnostic criteria (Hanifin's and UK Working Party) are helpful at ruling in disease when criteria are met; Hanifin's criteria are better at ruling out diagnosis when criteria are not met (). C
Diagnostic testing is seldom necessary for accurate diagnosis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Greasy, brown scale—scalp, ears, nose, eyebrows, sternal area
Erythematous patches, xerosis, burns—sites of exposure (usually hands)
Erythematous macules/patches with blisters/vesicles (plants); xerosis/lichenification if chronic—sites of exposure
Erythematous eruption in sun-exposed areas, most common in older individuals
Translucent quadrangular scales—extensor surfaces of arms/legs
Dry, fissured skin with scaling arms, legs
Sharply demarcated pink plaques with silvery scale—elbows, knees, scalp, intertriginous areas
May have erythematous patches and plaques with scale and resemble AD. CTCL may have a more truncal predominance and initial biopsies may be read as AD.

list.listitem: See for UK Working Party diagnostic criteria for AD (LR+ 21, LR− 0.15).
The REACH criteria (composed of 11 questions for parents) can rule out AD.
Most patients develop an itch-scratch-rash cycle, which is typical of AD.
Findings that best rule in AD, when present, are onset before age 2, visible flexural eczema, and history of itchy, dry skin.
Typically spares axillary and groin areas.
The hallmark clinical signs and symptoms are as described in the diagnostic criteria ().
In the vast majority of cases, no additional testing is needed.
Laboratory testing (including IgE levels) is seldom necessary.
Percutaneous skin testing is not helpful for diagnosis, but may be helpful for identifying disease triggers.
Skin scraping to exclude tinea or scabies infections is occasionally helpful.
Occasionally a 4 mm punch biopsy is needed to exclude CTCL or another diagnosis other than AD. This is very important when the presenting picture is that of erythroderma.
The diagnosis of AD is based on gathering appropriate history and physical findings to support the diagnosis.
There is no single historical or physical examination finding or laboratory test that is sufficient for the diagnosis of AD.
Affected areas, signs and most bothersome symptoms vary by geographic region and age.
Several diagnostic criteria exist. These criteria are based largely on the historical and physical findings, with little emphasis on invasive testing ().

Emollients and moisturizers are first-line treatment for the chronic management of patients with atopic dermatitis (AD); they are used for maintenace therapy and should be continued during acute flares. A

Use topical corticosteroids (TCS) as first-line treatment during acute flares in children and adults. Moderate - to high-potency TCS are more effective than low-potency TCS for moderate to severe AD. A

Another first-line option for treating flares and for maintenance, especially for sensitive skin (eg, face, anogenital, and intertriginous areas), is topical tacrolimus 0.1% ointment. It is as effective as moderate- to high-potency TCS, and is superior to pimecrolimus and low-potency TCS. A

Topical Janus-associated kinase (JAK) inhibitors, A topical phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE-4) inhibitors, B and topical aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) agonists B are second-line options for moderately severe AD but may be cost-prohibitive.

Subcutaneous dupilumab (interleukin-4/13 inhibitor) appears to be the most effective systemic treatment for refractory, moderate to severe AD but may be cost-prohibitive (US$2980 for one month of therapy, 9/2024, www.goodrx.com). A
JAK inhibitors are highly effective systemic therapies for moderate to severe and refractory AD but may be very cost-prohibitive. A
A short course of sedating antihistamines may be useful for patients with sleep disturbance and concomitant allergies. C

Treat all skin affected by AD with emollients applied daily to a few times a day to prevent dryness and pruritus. A quick lukewarm shower or bath prior to emollient application facilitates hydration of the skin. Bath additives do not improve AD.

Emollients and moisturizers are first-line treatment for the chronic management of patients with AD. They should be continued during treatment of acute flares. Emollients and moisturizers lengthen periods of remission, decrease flares, and reduce overall use of topical corticosteroids (TCS).
Low- to medium-potency TCS should be used for acute flares of AD in infants and children. Medium- to high-potency TCS can be used for acute flares of AD in adolescents and adults.
Use low-potency TCS to treat flares affecting the face and neck, and medium- to high-potency TCS for the trunk and extremities.

A 2022 Cochrane review concluded that high- and medium-potency TCS are more effective in treating AD flares as compared to low-potency TCS. Once daily as compared to twice daily application has similar efficacy.
Once to twice weekly use of low-potency TCS applied to commonly affected areas with daily emollient use is more effective in preventing flares than emollients alone.
High-potency fluorinated TCS should be avoided on the face, eyelids, genitals, intertriginous areas, and in infants to avoid local and systemic complications associated with TCS.
Acute flares should be treated until clear, usually requiring 10 to 21 days of TCS. Use high-potency TCS for the shortest duration possible.

Topical tacrolimus and pimecrolimus are safe and effective treatment options for adults and children over 2 years of age who do not respond to or are intolerant of TCS. They provide a steroid-sparing topical option for patients with AD.
Use TCIs for flare-ups or maintenance therapy, especially for sensitive areas like the face, anogenital and intertriginous areas.
Tacrolimus appears as effective as medium- to high-potency TCS, and is superior to low-potency TCS and pimecrolimus 1% cream.
Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment is better than tacrolimus 0.03% cream, reducing treatment failure by 18% per physician assessment (RR 0.82, 95% CI, 0.72-0.92).

A Cochrane network meta-analysis in 2024 concluded that high-potency TCS, topical tacrolimus 0.1%, and topical JAK inhibitors are the most effective topical anti-inflammatory therapies for AD, and that topical PDE-4 inhibitors and low-potency TCS are among the least effective.
Twice daily crisaborole 2% ointment is effective for mild to moderate AD in adults and children 3 months and older. Efficacy compared to TCS is uncertain.
60g tube of crisaborole costs $747 (www.goodrx.com, 6/2024.
Topical difamilast, a selective PDE-4 inhibitor, improves clinician assessment of atopic dermatitis at four weeks as compared to placebo vehicle.

Topical tapinarof is an aryl hydrocarbon receptor agonist, a relatively new class of small molecule immunomodulator. Tapinarof appears to improve moderate AD among adult and adolescents as compared to placebo.

In another study, topical tapinarof 1% cream once daily was more effective than vehicle cream in treating moderate to severe AD in the short term (8 weeks), based on an RCT involving 813 children (2 years and older) and adults. 80% of study participants were younger than 18 years. The treatment group showed significant improvement in the proportion of patients with an AD score of 0 (clear) or 1 (almost clear) and at least a 2-grade improvement from baseline compared to placebo (46% vs 16%; NNT = 3; 95% CI 2.8 - 4.2). Study discontinuation sfrom adverse events were similar between groups. A 60g tube of tapinarof is around $1,500 (www.goodrx.com, 3/2025).

A trial identified 103 children age 2 to 18 years with severe AD who had failed potent topical therapies. They were randomized to ciclosporin or methotrexate. Both medications were effective at 36 weeks, with ciclosporin showing a more rapid early reponse and methotrexate a more durable late response.
For refractory AD in adults, dupilumab, an IL-4 and IL-13 inhibitor, appears to be the most effective biologic and systemic therapy.

Subcutaneous dupilumab showed improved clinical responses in adults with moderate to severe AD who did not respond to topical therapies, without significant safety concerns. In a combined analysis of two studies with 671 patients randomized to placebo or two doses of dupilumab, the primary outcome of clear or nearly clear skin was achieved more often with active therapy (NNT = 6). There was also significant improvement in sleep, symptoms such as itch (peak improvement 16 weeks p <0.001), quality of life scores (p <0.05), anxiety and depression (p <0.05). However, the cost is very high (US$2980 for one month of therapy, 9/2024, www.goodrx.com).
Dupilumab improves clinical outcomes and quality of life among children age 6 to 11 years with severe AD inadequately controlled by topical therapy.

In 251 adolescents with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis, and RCT found that the the proportion with 75% or more improvement in the Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI-75) score was higher with dupilumab compared with placebo (38% given every 4 weeks, 41% given every 2 weeks, and 8% with placebo).

A meta-analysis of eight RCTs with 2706 AD patients treated with dupilumab with follow-up from 4 to 52 weeks showed no significant association with overall herpes virus infection (RR 1.16; 95% CI, 0.78-1.74) and overall infections (RR 0.98; 95% CI, 0.83-1.16).
Observational trials suggest dupilumab is well tolerated with conjunctivitis being the most commonly reported adverse event.

Patients with an excellent response to dupilumab in a randomized trial were rerandomized to either 300 mg every 1 to 2 weeks, every 4 weeks, every 8 weeks, or placebo. A dose response pattern was seen, although dosing every 4 weeks was very nearly as effective as every 1 to 2 weeks. This would be cost-saving and more convenient for patients.
Combined analysis of four RCT found that dupilumab injection every 2 weeks significantly reduced pruritis in both adults and adolescents by 2 days and 5 days, respectively.

A study of 215 patients with severe AD using topical therapy randomized participants age 13 and over to subcutaneous nemolizumab 60 mg (IL-31 inhibitor) or placebo. The percent responders was greater in the active treatment group (40% vs 22%, NNT = 6).A similar study found greater improvement in itch scores with nemolizumab in a study of 6 to 12 yeara olds with moderate to severe pruritus due to AD.

The IL-13 inhibiting monoclonal antibody tralokinumab was significantly more effective than placebo in two randomized trials in over 1600 adults with moderate to severe AD (EASI-75 25% vs 13% in trial 1 and 33% vs 11% in trial 2). Adverse events occurring at more often with tralokinumab were: viral URI, conjunctivitis, and injection-site reactions.

Omalizumab (Xolair), a monoclonal antibody that is an IgE antagonist, is more effective than placebo in alleviating symptoms in children 4 to 19 years of age with severe AD (SCORAD >/= 40) at 24 weeks but not at 48 weeks, based on a single-setting study in the U.K. involving 62 patients. Omalizumab 150mg costs $2580 per month (www.goodrx.com, 2/2023). It is FDA-approved for moderate to severe persistent asthma, chronic idiopathic urticaria, and nasal polyposis, but not for atopic dermatitis.
In a small study of patients with hand/foot AD, dupilumab improved symptoms and quality of life.
Dupilumab improved AD severity in children age 6 months to 6 years with causing significant adverse events.
The IL-13 inhibitor lebriki improved AD severity at 16 weeks weeks as compared to placebo for adults and adolescents with moderate or severe AD.
Topical JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib reduces severity and area of AD at 4 weeks as compared to placebo and appears to have similar efficacy as compared to triamcinolone cream.
Topical ruxolitinib improves pruritis within 36 hours and may be more effective than triamcinolone cream in improving pruritis at 4 weeks.

The topical JAK inhibitor delgocitinib appears to be effective for both adults and children >2 years with moderate to severe eczema. In an double-blinded, randomized trial of 137 children age 2-15 years with moderate to severe eczema, 0.25% delgocitinib ointment applied twice daily for four weeks improved eczema severity and pruritis as compared to vehicle. In a similar trial of 158 adults with moderate to severe eczema, twice daily application of 0.5% delgocitinib ointment improved eczema severity and pruritis at 4 weeks as compared to vehicle. The ointment appers to be safe for up to 52 weeks but many patients will require TCS rescue therapy. The medication is not yet available in the United States.

Oral once daily baricitinib 4 mg along with topical corticosteroids reduces the severity of AD among adults with poor response to TCS and emollients. Monthly cost of 30 tablets of the 2 mg dose is around $3100 (www.goodrx.com, 6/2024)

Patients (n = 329) with moderate to severe AD were randomized to the oral baricitinib 4 mg, 2 mg, or placebo in addition to use of TCS as needed for all. The primary outcome of Investigator Global Assessment (IGA) of clear or almost clear was seen in 31%, 24% and 15% respectively (p = 0.004 for the 4 mg group, p = 0.08 for 2 mg group vs placebo; NNT for 4 mg group = 7).

The oral JAK inhibitor abrocitinib was studied in an RCT with 391 patients, randomized to abrocitinib 200 mg, 100 mg, or placebo. IGA response was 38%, 28% and 9% respectively for the three groups. The drug was generally well tolerated.

A study of 901 patients with severe AD randomized adolescents and adults (age 12-75) to upadacitinib 15 mg daily, upadacitinib 30 mg daily, or placebo for 16 weeks. All received topical steroid in a step-down fashion. At 16 weeks, the percentage of patients with >75% improvement in eczema severity score were 64.6%, 77.1%, and 26.3%, respectively. Similar results were seen at 52 weeks. Adverse drug effects included acne, nasopharyngitis, and headaches. Discontinuation rates were low in all groups.

listitem.strong: Comparative trials involving different drug classes

list.listitem: A network meta-analysis of 83 RCTs involving 22,122 participants found abrocitinib 200 mg once daily and upadacitinib 30 mg once daily to be the most effective immunomodulators for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis. Dupilumab 600 mg then 300 mg every 2 weeks was comparable to upadacitinib 15 mg daily. Dupilumab, which was the most common comparator in studies, was better than abrocitinib 100 mg daily, baricitinib 4 mg and 2 mg daily, and tralokinumab 600 mg then 300 mg every 2 weeks. Both abrocitinib and upadacitinib cost over $5,000 per month (2/2023, www.goodrx.com).

A study randomized 838 patients unresponsive to topical therapies to abrocitinib 200 mg orally once daily, abrocitinib 100 mg once daily, dupilumab 300 mg every 2 weeks, or placebo. The IGA responses were 48.4%, 36.6%, 36.5%, and 14.0% respectively. All were better than placebo, and while abrocitinib 200 mg was better than dupilumab for the outcome of pruritis, in general there was no significant difference between the two active drugs.

A blinded study randomized 693 patients with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis to either dupilumab or the JAK inhibitor upadacitinib. After 4 months, more patients achieved EASI-75 in the upadacitinib (71% vs 61%, p = 0.006, NNT = 10). Upadacitinib was associated with a higher risk of superimposed infection (1.1% vs 0.6%), herpes zoster (2.0% vs 0.9%), and acne (15.8% vs 2.6%).

A trial compared upadacitinib (a JAK inhibitor) with dupilumab (a monoclonal against IL-4) in 930 adolescents with moderate to severe AD. The EASI 90 and WP-NRS 0/1 response was better with upadacitinib at 16 weeks (20% vs 9%, p = 0.001).
For patients with severe AD, guidelines recommend systemic dupilumab, tralokinumab, upadacitinib, abrocitinib, and baricitinib, in addition to topical agents.

Coal tar products appear to be therapeutic in AD, are well tolerated with few side effects, and are cost-effective based on a meta-analysis of four studies. Staining and odor are deterrents to coal tar therapy.
Topical antihistamines, such as doxepin, are not routinely recommended due to stinging and increased risk of contact dermatitis.
Probiotic supplementation may reduce investigator reported AD severity but not parent or patient reported symptom severity.
Oral H1 antihistamines as monotherapy or add-on therapy for AD is not supported by robust evidence.
Oral montelukast, a leukotriene inhibitor, does not appear to be effective for the treatment of AD.
Systemic antibiotics should be reserved for actively infected lesions.
Anti-staphylococcal treatments, including topical and oral antibiotics as well as bleach baths, have uncertain benefits in the treatment of infected or uninfected AD.
There is no evidence that evening primrose oil, borage oil, zinc, pyridoxine, vitamin D, vitamin E, Chinese herbal medicine, or other herbal therapy is effective for the treatment of AD.
Similarly, there is no evidence of effectiveness for homeopathy, saltwater baths, or massage therapy.

Behavioral modification therapy targeted toward habit-reversal techniques can decrease the habit of scratching in patients with AD and improves skin symptoms at 2 months, interfering with the scratch-itch-scratch cycle that perpetuates chronic AD.

In a single blinded small study of 39 children (median age 8 years) with mild, moderate, or severe AD, children were randomized to receive habit reversal training or usual care. Final assessment after 8 weeks showed improvement in symptoms and severity in both groups but larger improvement in intervention group (32 point vs 20 point at 8 weeks; p <0.001).
Mindfulness based therapy and self-compassion may improve quality of life and eczema severity among adults with AD.
Educational and psychological interventions for AD may be effective but the clinical significance of their effects are uncertain, based on a Cochrane review.
Optimal frequency of bathing remains unclear.

Twice daily bathing followed by application of emollients may improve symptoms as compared to twice weekly bathing. Another RCT (n = 438) found that frequency of bathing (daily versus weekly) has no impact on eczema symptoms for adults and children with moderate to severe eczema.

A randomised controlled trial of 483 children aged 1 to 11 years in 96 general practices in UK were randomised to oil-based emollient of their choice with bath water or usual care without bath oil emollient. The 7 point POEM scores improved in both groups equally from baseline over 16 weeks of treatment.
In the absence of a true IgE mediated allergy, dietary elimination is not recommended.
Egg-free diet may improve AD symptoms in symptomatic infants with egg-IgE positive antibodies.
House dust mite reduction and avoidance measures have uncertain benefits for the treatment of AD.
There is limited evidence supporting the use of specific allergen immunotherapy (SIT) for patients with AD.

For patients with more severe disease, phototherapy is an option. Based on low-certainty evidence, narrowband ultraviolet B (NB-UVB) results to better patient-reported symptoms, physician-rated signs, and IGA scores than placebo at 12 weeks.
Dietary elimination appears to minimally improve AD symptoms.
In a meta-analysis of 23 randomized trials allergen immmuno therapy (either sublingual or subcutaneous) improved AD severity and quality of life.

Hospitalization may be required for patients who appear erythrodermic or have widespread, severe skin disease resistant to outpatient therapy. These patients should have a 4 mm punch biopsy done to rule out CTCL and psoriasis.
Systemic antibiotics should be reserved for actively infected lesions.
Topical antibiotics may be appropriate for mild, locally infected lesions.
Sedating antihistamines should be reserved for patients with sleep disturbances associated with AD. Nonsedating antihistamines appear to have a very limited role in the treatment of AD.
Melatonin may be effective in improving sleep quality in children with few side effects.
Removal of the patient from environmental allergens or emotional stressors, intense patient education, and compliance with medication therapy may result in sustained improvement in AD.
Wet wraps for severe AD flares have unclear clinical benefit as compared to usual care with topical therapies alone.
Skin clearing in the hospitalized patient allows allergen skin testing and controlled provocative challenges to identify potential triggers.
AD is notable for its relapsing/remitting course. The interval between exacerbations is variable. C
The majority of children with AD outgrow the condition by adolescence. C
Early-onset disease (<2 years) is more likely to be persistent throughout early childhood. C
In children with onset of AD prior to 2 years of age, 20% will have persistent symptoms of disease and 17% will have intermittent symptoms of disease by the age of 7. B
In infants with AD, 35% will develop asthma later in life. B
Atopic dermatitis is consistently associated with asthma, food allergy, and other autoimmune skin conditions. B
Expert guidelines suggest most topical therapies such as moisturizers, TCS, tacrolimus, and antiseptics such as chlorhexidine and sodium hypochlorite (bleach) are safe in pregnancy and lactation.
Topical agents should be applied after breastfeeding. Nipples should be gently cleansed prior to feeding.
Phototherapy should be considered for uncontrolled AD during pregnancy and lactation.
Systemic therapies should not be routinely prescribed for pregnant or lactating patients.
See modified criteria for diagnosis of AD in infants.

feature.caption: UK Working Party Diagnostic Criteria for Atopic Dermatitis.
feature.feature_body:
Pruritus (or parent report of such) plus three or more of the following features:
• History of flexural involvement (or cheeks in child <10yo)
• Personal history of asthma or hay fever (or history of atopy in first-degree relative if <4yo)
• History of generalized dry skin within the past year (visible)
• Flexural eczema (cheeks, forehead, outer limbs in child <4yo)
• Onset of rash in child younger than 2yo (not used in child <4 yo)
Adapted from Williams HC, Burney PG, Pembroke AC, Hay RJ. The U.K. Working Party's Diagnostic Criteria for Atopic Dermatitis. III. Independent hospital validation. Br J Dermatol 1994;131:406–416.
